issues.subcategory: results-based conclusions from dummy data
issues.description: The manuscript presents simulated/randomized data as if they were study findings, yet repeatedly discusses them as substantive replication outcomes and draws theoretical conclusions from them. This makes the reported results uninterpretable as evidence about the phenomenon and creates a major inconsistency between the stated status of the data and the inferential language used throughout the abstract and results.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.] ... We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: methods/results use nonexistent data as sample
issues.description: The participants section reports 1000 generated Qualtrics responses with demographic characteristics as though they were actual participants, despite stating these are simulated data. This undermines the integrity of the methods and results because no real sample was analyzed.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.subcategory: analysis of random simulated data
issues.description: All inferential statistics reported in the results are computed on randomized dummy data generated to simulate output formatting. Statistical tests, p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes from such data have no evidential meaning and should not be reported as study results.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.subcategory: causal/theoretical claims from dummy data
issues.description: The abstract and results interpret simulated data as showing support or lack of support for hypotheses and theoretical mechanisms. Because the data are random placeholders rather than observations from the described experiment, no causal or empirical conclusions can be drawn.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: not a close replication due to major design changes
issues.description: The manuscript labels the study a 'close to very close replication' despite substantial deviations from the original: merging two original studies into one experiment, adding intervention to the joint condition, moving from real to hypothetical donation, collecting affect measures in the joint condition, changing stimuli, and changing the participant pool and setting. These changes alter both manipulation structure and dependent measures enough that direct comparability is compromised.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition... Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5... instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: hypothetical donation substituted for real donation
issues.description: The original studies involved consequential donation behavior using money participants possessed. The replication replaces this with an 'imaginary donation' from $0 to $5, which may measure stated intention or hypothetical generosity rather than actual helping behavior. This weakens construct validity and comparability to the target finding.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: different intervention structure than original studies
issues.description: The replication changes the operationalization of the independent variable by embedding explicit and implicit manipulations in one 2 x 3 design and applying explicit intervention to the joint condition. This changes the psychological meaning of the conditions and makes the original hypotheses only partially comparable.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single between-subject design... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.subcategory: extension measure not aligned with stated prediction
issues.description: The extension hypothesis predicts higher perceived impact for identifiable than statistical victims, but the reported significant post-hoc comparison is between statistical and joint conditions, not identifiable versus statistical. The operationalized comparison does not support the stated construct-level hypothesis.
issues.quote: It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims. ... Significant differences were found between the statistical victim condition and the joint condition...

issues.subcategory: contradictory effect size sign in post-hoc test
issues.description: The reported t statistic for Identifiable vs Statistical is negative, which ordinarily indicates the first group mean is lower than the second if computed as first minus second. However, the text interprets the opposite, and the reported Cohen's d is positive. This sign inconsistency suggests either coding/reporting errors or misinterpretation of the comparison direction.
issues.quote: Identifiable VS Statistical | 994 | -2.40 | 0.13 | 0.076 | [-0.05, 0.20] | .049* ... participants who faced an identifiable victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the statistical victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: confidence interval inconsistent with significant effect size
issues.description: For the significant post-hoc comparison, the reported Cohen's d is positive (0.076) but its 95% CI includes negative values [-0.05, 0.20]. While this can occur for very small effects, the mismatch combined with the negative t and positive interpretation raises concern that confidence intervals and effect size directions were not computed consistently.

issues.subcategory: incorrect claim of no significant effect despite significant interaction
issues.description: The text states 'no significant effect was found on intervention but the identifiability and the interaction effect ... was supported' and later interprets only the identifiable-versus-statistical difference, but does not probe the significant interaction appropriately. A significant interaction means main effects are difficult to interpret marginally without simple-effects analyses.
issues.quote: Results from Table 9 showed that no significant effect was found on intervention but the identifiability and the interaction effect of identifiability and intervention was supported.

issues.subcategory: inappropriate/simple contrast not aligned with factorial interaction
issues.description: After finding a significant 2 x 3 interaction, the manuscript conducts a t-test comparing the identifiable/no-intervention condition to the combination of all other five conditions. This omnibus contrast is not a standard or clearly justified decomposition of the interaction in the current design and pools heterogeneous conditions, making interpretation difficult and increasing arbitrariness.
issues.quote: Given the significant interaction effect, we also conducted a t-test to study if the mean of identifiable/no intervention condition is different from the mean of combining other five conditions on donation.

issues.subcategory: conditional post-hoc testing plan
issues.description: The analysis plan specifies post-hoc tests only if interactions are significant and pairwise tests only if main effects/significant effects occur. This selective follow-up is common, but the broader plan includes multiple possible analyses, contrasts, and outcomes without clear familywise control across the full hypothesis set, leaving substantial flexibility in which results are highlighted.
issues.quote: Post-hoc contrast test (Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant) ... Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons (Note: We conduct the test only if the effect of identifiability and intervention are significant)

issues.subcategory: multiple testing without adequate correction across outcomes
issues.description: The manuscript tests multiple ANOVAs across aggregated feelings and six segregated feelings (including the extension), plus multiple post-hoc comparisons and correlations across six conditions. Only some pairwise tests are Bonferroni adjusted; there is no overall multiplicity strategy across the large family of hypothesis tests, inflating Type I error.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on segregated affective reactions...

issues.subcategory: treating bounded ordinal/count donation as ANOVA outcome without justification
issues.description: Donation is measured as an integer amount from $0 to $5, a bounded discrete variable with only six values. The original study reportedly also used ordered probit regression, but the replication drops that analysis and relies on ANOVA/t-tests without justification, assumption checks, or robustness analyses. This may distort inference if distributions are non-normal or heteroskedastic.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 ... Ordered probit regression ... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: missing assumption checks for ANOVA/t-tests
issues.description: No information is provided about checking homogeneity of variance, normality/residual diagnostics, independence concerns, or robustness of parametric tests, despite using ANOVA and multiple t-tests on bounded donation scores and Likert-type feeling measures.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI given that such function is not available for ANOVA testing in JAMOVI.

issues.subcategory: aggregated feelings measure unspecified and unvalidated
issues.description: The manuscript analyzes 'aggregated feelings' but does not explain how the composite was constructed, whether items were averaged or summed, whether reverse coding was needed, or whether the scale had acceptable internal consistency. Without this, the aggregate's meaning and reliability are unclear.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: missing item wording and scale anchors for outcomes
issues.description: The exact wording, response scales, anchor labels, and scoring of key dependent variables (feeling items, perceived impact, donation appropriateness, etc.) are not reported in the manuscript. This prevents evaluation of construct validity and reproducibility.
issues.quote: These items included the feeling of being upset, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, and the appropriateness of donation to help the victims.

issues.subcategory: randomization procedure insufficiently described
issues.description: The manuscript states participants 'will be assigned randomly' but gives no details on allocation mechanism, block structure, Qualtrics randomizer logic, or whether assignment was equal/probability balanced. Such details are needed to assess implementation fidelity.
issues.quote: Participants will be assigned randomly to the intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: manipulation materials not described in manuscript
issues.description: The explicit intervention and victim-information stimuli are central manipulations, yet their content is not described in sufficient detail in the paper itself. Reliance on external links and supplementary files is not enough for readers to evaluate what participants actually saw.
issues.quote: For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below...

issues.subcategory: absence of manipulation checks
issues.description: The study tests whether explicit and implicit manipulations induce deliberative thinking or awareness of the identifiable victim effect, but no manipulation checks are described. Without verifying that the manipulations changed the intended psychological state, null or positive findings are hard to interpret.
issues.quote: The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.subcategory: joint condition does not isolate implicit deliberation cleanly
issues.description: The manuscript assumes that presenting both identifiable and statistical information 'implicitly' activates calculation/deliberation, but this condition also changes information amount, salience, and comparative framing. Any differences may reflect these confounds rather than deliberation per se.
issues.quote: The victim statistics was believed to eliminate the identifiable victim effect implicitly in the joint condition as reflected in the donation towards the identifiable victim.

issues.subcategory: mischaracterization of original effect and debiasing logic
issues.description: The manuscript at times frames the effect as deliberation reducing motivation to help a single identified beneficiary because such help is less effective. This imports an efficacy/utilitarian rationale that may not cleanly follow from the original manipulation and risks conflating reduced affect, moral reasoning, and perceived effectiveness.
issues.quote: Reasoning about the choice of donation may suppress people’s automatic affective reaction towards the identifiable victim due to the perceived lack of effectiveness when contributing their money to a single individual.

issues.subcategory: sample/source mismatch with overclaim of replication
issues.description: The original study used participants in a university student center in Pennsylvania, whereas the replication plans MTurk workers online. This major contextual and demographic shift is acknowledged but insufficiently incorporated into interpretive claims about direct replication and reproducibility.
issues.quote: Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: dummy sample demographics implausible and noninformative
issues.description: The reported average age of 67.8 (range 18-120) is implausible for MTurk and clearly reflects random generation rather than a realistic target population. As presented, these demographics cannot inform generalizability and further underscore that the reported sample is not meaningful.
issues.quote: Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10 ... Age range (years) | 18-120

issues.subcategory: pre-registration details incomplete/inaccessible in manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript asserts preregistration and open-science compliance but does not summarize key preregistered hypotheses, exclusion criteria, stopping rules, or analysis decisions in enough detail in the article. It also includes placeholder text ('OSF pre-registration review:.') and unfinished links, which weakens transparency.
issues.quote: OSF pre-registration review:. ... Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here> Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.subcategory: deviations from original analyses without clear justification
issues.description: The replication departs from the original analytic strategy by omitting ordered probit regression, adding analyses for the joint/intervention cells, and adding multiple feeling outcomes. These changes create analytic flexibility and complicate direct comparison unless strongly justified and preregistered in detail.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression ... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: no reporting of exclusion criteria implementation/attention checks
issues.description: The manuscript says there was no exclusion of samples, but because this is an online survey with emotionally and cognitively relevant manipulations, readers need to know whether attention checks, duplicate checks, bot screening, or incomplete-response handling were used or intentionally omitted.
issues.quote: There was no exclusion of samples in this study.

issues.subcategory: missing data handling not specified
issues.description: There is no information on whether any items could be skipped, how missing responses would be handled, whether complete-case analysis was used, or whether the simulated data simply contain no missingness. This omission matters especially for multi-item feeling scales and online data collection.
issues.quote: There was no exclusion of samples in this study.

issues.subcategory: power analysis not aligned with actual focal tests
issues.description: Power was based on the smallest original effect of intervention (d = -0.36), but the actual design is a 2 x 3 factorial with interactions, post-hoc contrasts, and additional outcomes. Powering on a simple d from the original study may not ensure adequate power for the redesigned interaction tests or extension hypotheses.
issues.quote: Given the smallest effect size regarding the effect of intervention... with Cohens’d = -0.36, the corresponding sample size to detect such effect was 314.

issues.subcategory: power analysis based on original effect from changed design
issues.description: The manuscript uses an effect size from the original 2 x 2 context to justify sample size in a merged 2 x 3 design with different operationalizations and a hypothetical donation DV. The original effect size is not directly transportable to the current design parameters.
issues.quote: To obtain the minimal sample size required for this study, a power analysis was conducted using Gpower... Given the smallest effect size... was d = -0.36... sample size... 314.

issues.subcategory: hypothesis numbering and interpretation mismatch
issues.description: Hypothesis 4 is described as 'Implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donations to an identifiable victim,' but the design operationalizes implicit learning via a joint condition and also applies explicit intervention to that joint condition. This blurs the distinction between H3 and H4 and makes the hypothesis mapping to conditions unclear.
issues.quote: 4 (Interaction effect) | Implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donations to an identifiable victim

issues.subcategory: extension hypothesis contradicted by abstract and results framing
issues.description: The introduction predicts higher perceived impact for identifiable than statistical victims, but the abstract states lower perceived impact when faced with an identifiable victim or joint condition, and the results only support statistical > joint. The manuscript therefore presents inconsistent directional predictions and conclusions.
issues.quote: It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims. ... Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: table numbering/order inconsistency
issues.description: The manuscript refers to 'Table 7 summarizes the current replication as a close to very close replication' but the actual classification table is labeled Table 6, while later Table 7 is descriptive statistics. Such inconsistencies hinder interpretation and suggest insufficient internal checking.
issues.quote: Figure 2 specifies the classification of the replications... Table 7 summarizes the current replication as a "close to very close replication". ... Table 6 Classification of the replication...

issues.subcategory: sample size reporting inconsistency in comparison table
issues.description: Table 4 appears to repeat the '1000' sample size and duplicate columns/entries, making the comparison between original and replication unclear. This suggests table construction problems that reduce confidence in reporting accuracy.
issues.quote: Table 4 ... Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.subcategory: no cell-wise actual Ns/planned allocation rationale
issues.description: Although the simulated tables show approximately balanced cell sizes, the methods do not report the intended target N per cell or whether equal allocation was enforced. This is especially important for a 2 x 3 design with interaction tests.
issues.quote: Table 7 ... Intervention condition | 2.58 [1.77] (159) | 2.46 [1.69] (175) | 2.37 [1.62] (166) ... No intervention condition | ...

issues.subcategory: misleading emphasis on p=.049 after Bonferroni with trivial effect
issues.description: The only significant donation post-hoc contrast after Bonferroni has p=.049 and an extremely small effect size (d≈.08), yet the narrative treats it as supporting the identifiability effect. This overstates an effect that is practically negligible even within the simulated data.
issues.quote: Identifiable VS Statistical | ... d | 0.076 ... pBonferroni | .049* ... meaning that participants who faced an identifiable victim ... tended to donate more

issues.subcategory: overreliance on identifiable victim effect significance despite tiny meta-analytic effect
issues.description: The manuscript argues strongly for the importance of the effect while citing a meta-analytic mean effect size of only 0.05. The discussion does not reconcile this tiny effect with claims about the phenomenon's robustness or practical importance, nor with the rationale for expecting medium effects from the target study.
issues.quote: Although the overall mean effect size was only 0.05, the significance of the identifiable victim effect is still crucial...

issues.subcategory: lack of blinding and demand characteristics risk
issues.description: The explicit intervention teaches participants about the identifiable victim effect before measuring donation tendency, making hypothesis awareness and demand characteristics highly likely. The manuscript does not discuss whether this threatens the interpretation of reduced donations as deliberation rather than compliance.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims

issues.subcategory: correlational analyses treated as predictive mechanism evidence
issues.description: The manuscript uses correlations between aggregated feelings and donation to assess whether affective feelings 'predict' donation, but such within-condition correlations are observational and cannot establish that feelings causally drive donation. Shared method variance and reverse causality remain possible.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.subcategory: missing reliability for feeling scales
issues.description: No Cronbach's alpha, omega, or other reliability estimate is reported for the aggregated feelings composite or for any multi-item construct. Without reliability information, attenuation and interpretability of null findings are unclear.
issues.quote: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: unclear coding/scoring of joint-condition donation target
issues.description: In the joint condition, it is unclear whether participants donate to the identified victim, to both victim types, or make a single overall donation judgment. Because the original study's joint presentation had a specific comparative logic, precise scoring here is essential for interpretation.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) ... The joint condition group would also be required to fill up the questionnaire...

issues.subcategory: updated victim information may alter emotional intensity
issues.description: Using updated victim information from Save the Children instead of the original materials may meaningfully change sympathy, vividness, identifiability, and perceived need. This threatens construct equivalence, especially in a paradigm highly sensitive to stimulus framing.
issues.quote: We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.
